initial_observation.encounter_context: Presented to an ophthalmological department of a hospital in Switzerland with diplopia for 3 months
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: Orthoptic diagnostics demonstrated a presumed congenital paresis of the left IVth cranial nerve with exophoria, hyperopia and astigmatism on both sides and presbyopia with good visual acuity
known_prior_history: No relevant medical history was known
Had not been abroad in the last years
Did not take any illicit drugs

evidence_items.source_text: 8 months later, the patient presented at a private neurological practice due to recurrent diplopia accompanied by pain in his pelvis radiating to his right leg, urge incontinence and symptoms of a sensory polyneuropathy on his lower limbs. Furthermore, a left VIth cranial nerve palsy, decreased deep tendon reflexes, reduced sense of vibration and an unsteady gait were documented in the records. While electrophysiological examination and laboratory results including screening for Lyme disease and vasculitis were unremarkable, an MRI showed cervical spinal cord stenosis. Decompression surgery was recommended, but was declined by the patient.

During the subsequent 9 months, visual acuity deteriorated considerably to a Snellen fraction of less than 20/200 on the right side and 25/100 on the left side. Concomitant bilateral cataracts and significant atrophy of the optic nerve (right>left) were documented. Bilateral cataract surgery was performed in a private practice without any amelioration of visual acuity. A tumour or inflammatory alterations of the optic nerve were ruled out by a brain MRI. A genetic panel for >100 genes related to hereditary optic atrophy including Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy was also unrevealing.

One year later, the patient presented again at a neurological private practice due to further progression of his ataxia. Furthermore, a prominent relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) was found. A repeated MRI scan showed regression of the formerly described herniated disc without any signs of myelopathy. Laboratory rheumatological screening (antineuronal antibodies) and tumour markers were unremarkable again. Electrophysiological testing did not show any clear evidence for the presence of a polyneuropathy.

4 years after his first symptoms with extensive but unsuccessful diagnostics and treatments, including several MRIs, broad genetic analysis and multiple eye surgeries, he was referred to our neurological department for further evaluation. On referral, the patient suffered from severe gait ataxia due to diminished proprioception and absent deep tendon reflexes. Furthermore, diminished pupillary reflex to light with preserved constriction during convergence, described as an Argyll-Robertson pupil as well as an almost complete loss of vision were found. Syphilis screening test was positive, which was confirmed by serological confirmation tests and positive CSF studies (see ‘Investigations’). On further interrogation, the patient disclosed a previous syphilis infection 30 years ago, which was likely treated insufficiently with an unknown oral antibiotic. Exact route or place of infection were not recallable. Due to the patient’s history and clinical findings along with the laboratory results confirming serological and CSF syphilis activity, we were able to establish the diagnosis of tabes dorsalis.

A laboratory screening was conducted and revealed positive titres for a syphilis screening test. The diagnosis of syphilis was further confirmed by positive T. pallidum haemagglutination assay and serological activity with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) of 1:8. A CSF study revealed pleocytosis with 93 cells/µL, predominantly mononuclear, elevated protein, albumin and lactate as well as an intrathecal synthesis of IgG-directed against T. pallidum (table 1).

After the diagnosis was confirmed, the patient received penicillin G 4 million International units (IU) intravenously six times per day for 14 days according to current guidelines.8 9 After an initial 4 days of inpatient intravenous therapy the patient was switched to an outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy via an antibiotic pump with pencillin G 24 million IU per day for the remaining days of the 14-day regimen. To additionally account for a possible need of a longer duration of treatment in later stages of infection (such as for late latent syphilis), one shot of long-acting Benzathine-Penicillin 2.4 million IU intramuscularly was added after the intravenous therapy.7

6 months after treatment, the patient did not notice any significant clinical amelioration. Visual acuity was still <20/200 on the right side and 20/100 on the left side. Also the ataxia had not changed. We were, however, able to demonstrate an improvement of the laboratory markers. In cerebrospinal fluid, mononuclear pleocytosis decreased from 93 to 12 cells/µL, protein levels decreased from 1.65 to 0.79 g/L and albumin decreased from 0.89 to 0.43 g/L. Furthermore, serological activity also decreased to a Treponema RPR of 1:2 after 9 months, which fulfils most current guidelines’ criteria for an adequate response to treatment (table 2).
